How to read this model

The 3D surfaces show schematic angular shapes, based on real spherical harmonics. Size is normalized for comparison; radial nodes and multi-electron radial functions are not rendered. These are not electron paths.

Two shades distinguish wavefunction phase, not electric charge. Boxes use a Hund’s-rule filling model: one electron per orbital before pairing, with opposite spins in a pair. The choice of real orbital basis and pairing order is illustrative.

Electron count alone does not establish an element’s charge or confirm its ground state. Input accepts s, p, d, and f subshells with shell numbers 1–20.

Sources: OpenStax orbital shapes, electron configurations, and angular functions.

HOW TO EXPLORE

A little curiosity goes a long way.

Move through the world

Drag to orbit, Shift-drag or right-drag to pan, and scroll to zoom. On touch screens, use one finger to rotate and two fingers to pan or pinch. Click or tap a card to approach it and open its profile. “Back to view” returns to where you were; “Overview” fits the formation.

Explore with a keyboard

Focus the world with Tab. Arrow keys orbit; Shift + arrows pan. + and − zoom, R fits the formation, and Escape closes a profile and returns to the previous view. Use the Element list or search results to select any element with Tab and Enter. Layouts and filters also work with a keyboard.

Four ways to see the same elements

The Table shows conventional groups and periods. Helix, Sphere, and Grid are spatial visualizations; they do not change chemical relationships. The separate lanthanide and actinide rows belong to periods 6 and 7.

Build an electron configuration

Open Orbitals, enter a configuration such as 1s2 2s2 2p4 or [Ar] 3d6 4s2, and choose Visualize configuration. Choose an occupied subshell, then an orbital box to explore its shape and occupancy. Shapes are angular models, with radial nodes omitted; use “How to read this model” for the scientific notes.

Pink outlines mark the s-block (including helium), orange the d-block, blue the p-block, and purple the detached f-block series. The f-series include all lanthanides and actinides in this compact layout; the placement of their end elements varies by convention.

Numbers tell a story

The atomic number counts protons. A neutral atom has the same number of electrons. The period is its horizontal row. Main-group valence counts use the outer shell; transition-metal counts include s and d electrons.

Scientific notes & sources

Atomic masses use the CIAAW abridged standard atomic weights, including the 2024 revisions, with uncertainties shown in each profile. These are averages for normal terrestrial materials; individual isotopes have different masses. Standard atomic weight is dimensionless; its numerical value gives the corresponding average atomic mass in u.

Bracketed integers come from the IUPAC May 2022 periodic table. They identify the mass number (protons + neutrons) of the isotope with the longest confirmed half-life in that edition, not a standard atomic weight or exact isotope mass.

Valence conventions follow OpenStax’s electron-configuration discussion. For d-block elements we show the formal s + d count; it is not a bond count or oxidation state. For lanthanides and actinides we show the outermost-shell count; f and d electrons can also participate in bonding. Lawrencium uses the 7s²7p¹ ground-state assignment.

Categories are an educational convention: group 12 is included with the transition metals, polonium with post-transition metals, and astatine with halogens. Superheavy-element categories and main-group valence counts follow table position; their chemistry is not fully established. See the Royal Society of Chemistry for individual references.

Rendering quality adapts to your screen and device. System reduced-motion preferences are respected.
